The railway network under London, which began on 10 January 1863 when the Metropolitan Railway opened between Paddington and Farringdon. It was the world's first underground railway.

London's streets were jammed with horses, carts and people walking in from the new main line stations at the edge of the city. The answer was to dig a trench under the roads, lay track, and roof it over again, a method called cut and cover. The first trains were pulled by steam engines, with gas lit wooden carriages, and smoke filled the tunnels.

Deeper lines followed, bored through the London clay as round tubes, which gave the system its nickname. In 1933 the lines were brought under one public body, and Harry Beck's diagram map became a model for transit maps everywhere.

The Underground let London spread into suburbs. Other cities copied it, from Budapest and Paris to the Moscow Metro and Tokyo's Ginza Line. It grew alongside the city's role as world financial centre.
